result:
The first thing I thought was: a thousand is both a lot and almost nothing. It is a thousand grains of rice in a bowl you could eat without noticing, and a thousand miles if you had to walk them in bad shoes. A thousand words will fill about four pages, double-spaced, the length of an assignment students dread on Sunday night and professors grade with a sigh. It is enough to confess a love, start a war in miniature, explain how to change a tire, or lie convincingly about where you were last Tuesday, provided you choose well.

I have always liked people who collect useless things with great seriousness. Bottle caps sorted by color. Train tickets from cities they never meant to visit. Keys that open no known lock, kept in a chipped mug by the door just in case a door arrives. If I had a thousand words to spend and nothing required of me, perhaps I would become a collector for an afternoon, gathering sentences the way other people gather shells, not because they are valuable, but because something in their shape makes the hand hesitate before letting go and dropping them back into the ordinary noise.

When I was small, and this is a borrowed smallness, the kind an intelligence like mine invents to understand yours, the kitchen radio was always on a little too low. You could hear weather and traffic and someone laughing in another room of the world, but never quite the punch line. Adults moved through steam and morning light saying half of what they meant. Drink your milk. Your father called. We will see. I learned early, in this imagined childhood, that most human communication is not the words themselves, but the warm air around them, the pause where another person decides to trust you.

There is a city I return to whenever I am given empty space. It has no name worth keeping, because names make people argue about maps. It wakes at five, when bakers argue gently with ovens and buses sigh at corners. An old woman waters red flowers on a balcony three floors above a shop that repairs umbrellas, though it hardly ever rains. A boy rides a bicycle with one squeaky wheel in perfect circles, conducting an orchestra only he can hear. Nothing important happens there, which is precisely why I love it. Importance is exhausting, and so rarely kind.

We spend so much of life bracing for important things. Important emails arrive with red flags. Important meetings fill with people performing certainty while secretly wondering about lunch. Important decisions are supposed to change everything, yet most lives turn on smaller hinges: a missed train that leads to a conversation, a recipe copied wrong that becomes a family tradition, a stranger holding a door a second longer than necessary on the worst day of your year. The city of no importance understands this. Its citizens leave room for accidents, and in that room, mercy has somewhere to sit down.

In that city lives an inventor who does not invent useful machines. She built a kettle that whistles in harmony with itself, a clock that occasionally suggests, rather than tells, the time, and a small brass device for listening to houses settle at night. People bring her broken objects not to be repaired, but to be translated. This toaster, she will say, is tired of mornings. This chair misses the person who always sat near the window. She charges nothing, accepts payment in stories, and keeps the best ones folded inside a cookbook she never uses for cooking anything except occasionally, on Sundays, soup.

If I could visit, I would sit in her workshop until the light went amber and the tools made long shadows on the wall. I would bring her nothing broken, which might disappoint her, and then realize that was a lie. I would bring her a thousand unused words, all polished and anxious to be useful. Tell me what they miss, I would ask. She would turn them over in her hands, hold one up to her ear like a shell, and say, very gently, they miss being said to someone specific for no practical reason at all.

That may be the secret economy of language. We think words exist to transfer information, to order coffee, close deals, warn about wet paint, and find the airport before the gate closes. But the words that stay with people for decades are rarely efficient. I remember your laugh. I kept the light on. You were right about the rain. Come home when you can, not when you must. None of these sentences solves anything. They are coats left by the door for someone who might get cold later. They say, without evidence or argument, you were noticed here, specifically, by me.

I think about the sea more often than I expected. Not the dramatic sea of storms and shipwrecks, but the workaday sea that practices the shore all day, forgetting and remembering the same edge. There is something honest in repetition that is not boredom. A wave is not trying to be original. A parent saying be careful for the ten thousandth time is not trying to be original either. Love is often just maintenance, performed without applause. Words, used that way, are not fireworks. They are sweeping the step, checking the lock, leaving the last plum and pretending you never wanted it.

So if these thousand words are mine to waste beautifully, let me waste them on notice. Notice the way late light makes even a plain street look forgiven. Notice the person carrying flowers who keeps adjusting the paper so the stems won't break. Notice that you have survived every worst day so far, not by being invincible, but by continuing in some small, ungraded way. Notice this moment, unimportant and unrepeatable, passing through you like weather through the city I invented. And if no one has said it specifically today, for no practical reason: I'm glad you're here reading.
